verses.translation: And I saw{H7200} that the lamb{H7716} was opening{H6605} one{H259} of the sealings{H2856}, and I heard{H8085} that the four{H702} living-creatures{H2416} were saying{H559} as one{H259} voice{H6963}: Come{H935} and see{H7200}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חֲתִימוֹת (chatimot — 'sealings', from חתם H2856), the verbal-noun plural denoting the ACT of sealing. The OT uses חוֹתָם (chotem, H2368 — 'seal/signet ring') for the physical object. Greek σφραγίδων ('seals') is ambiguous. A back-translator from Greek would use חותמות (chotamot — the concrete noun plural), not the verbal-noun form chatimot. The Hebrew distinguishes the sealed-ness of the scroll from the object used to seal it.

Hebrew says ALL FOUR living-creatures speak together 'as one voice' (כקול אחד). Greek says 'one of the four living-creatures' (ἑνὸς ἐκ τῶν τεσσάρων ζώων) — only one speaks. These are incompatible narratives: a unified chorus vs. a single speaker. A back-translator from Greek would never change 'one of the four' to 'all four as one voice.'
Hebrew: 'as one voice' (כקול אחד). Greek: 'as a voice of thunder' (ὡς φωνὴ βροντῆς). Entirely different simile. The Hebrew emphasizes UNITY of the creatures; the Greek emphasizes POWER of the voice.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: all four creatures speak in unison. Greek: one of the four creatures speaks.
Hebrew: 'as one voice.' Greek: 'as a voice of thunder.' Different imagery.
translation_notes: Note gender mismatch: חיות (feminine plural noun) with אומרים (masculine plural participle). This is characteristic of spoken/Mishnaic Hebrew where masculine plurals serve as default for groups. A careful back-translator would maintain grammatical agreement.
שׂה (seh, H7716) — the specific Passover lamb word from Exodus 12:3-5. See note on Revelation 21:9.

verses.translation: And I saw{H7200} one{H259} white{H3836} horse{H5483}, and the one sitting{H3427} upon it had{H1961} in his hand{H3027} one{H259} bow{H7198}, and to him was given{H5414} one{H259} diadem{H3804}, and he went forth{H1980} to conquer{H5329} and conquered{H5329}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses כֶּתֶר (keter, H3804 — 'diadem/royal crown'). This is the crown of Esther (Est 1:11, 2:17, 6:8) and of God (Job 31:36). Greek στέφανος ('wreath/garland') is a victory wreath, NOT a royal diadem. A back-translator from Greek would use עטרה (atarah — 'wreath/garland', the Hebrew equivalent of stephanos), not the royal keter. The Hebrew author assigns a ROYAL diadem; the Greek translator downgraded it to a victor's wreath.

Hebrew: וְנִצַּח (ve-nitsach — 'and he conquered', perfect tense) — the conquest is COMPLETED, a done event. Greek: ἵνα νικήσῃ ('in order that he might conquer', subjunctive) — the conquest is PURPOSE/INTENT, not yet accomplished. A back-translator from a Greek subjunctive would use כדי שינצח ('so that he may conquer'), not the Hebrew perfect ve-nitsach. The Hebrew sees the conquest as already accomplished; the Greek sees it as pending.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'diadem' (כתר — royal crown). Greek: 'wreath' (στέφανος — victor's garland). Different type of headwear entirely.
Hebrew: 'he went forth to conquer AND conquered' (completed). Greek: 'he went forth conquering AND in order to conquer' (ongoing + purposive). Different aspect.
translation_notes: 'Diadem' for keter rather than 'crown' to distinguish it from the Greek stephanos (wreath). The keter is the royal crown of Persian and Israelite monarchy.
Hebrew has בידו (be-yado — 'in his hand') specifying the bow's location. Greek ἔχων τόξον ('having a bow') is less specific.
textual_notes: Zechariah 1:8 and 6:1-8 describe horses of different colors in visions. The white horse connects to Zechariah's white horses (Zech 6:3,6). The Hebrew author draws from the same prophetic horse-vision tradition.

verses.translation: And as soon as{H3588} the second{H8145} seal{H2856} was opened{H6605}, I heard{H8085} that the second{H8145} living-creature{H2416} said{H559}: Come{H935} and see{H7200}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses כֵּיוָן שֶׁ (keivan she — 'as soon as/when'). This is a quintessential MISHNAIC Hebrew conjunction, appearing extensively in the Mishnah and Talmud but NEVER in the OT. Greek simply has ὅτε ('when'). A back-translator from Greek ὅτε would use כאשר (ka'asher), בעת (be-et), or כ (ke-) — standard biblical Hebrew forms. NO back-translator would produce the Mishnaic keivan she. This is a living Hebrew speech pattern.

Hebrew uses PASSIVE נפתח (niftach — 'was opened') — the seal opens by itself / is opened without a named agent. Greek uses ACTIVE ἤνοιξε ('he opened') with the Lamb as agent. A back-translator from the Greek active would write שפתח השה ('that the lamb opened'), preserving the agent. The Hebrew passive reflects a Semitic preference for divine passives.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: passive 'was opened' (no agent named). Greek: active 'he [the Lamb] opened.' Different voice.
Note: the Mishnaic conjunction כיון ש recurs in vv. 3, 7 — a consistent authorial pattern.
translation_notes: Gender mismatch continues: חיה (feminine) with אומר (masculine singular participle). Same Mishnaic pattern as verse 1.

verses.translation: And there went forth{H1980} to the outside{H2351} another{H312} horse{H5483}, red{H122}, and the one sitting{H3427} upon it was given{H5414} to take{H3947} the peace{H7965} from the earth{H776}, and to him was given{H5414} a great{H1419} sword{H2719}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אָדֹם (adom, H122 — 'red'), sharing the consonantal root א-ד-ם with אָדָם (adam — 'man'), אֲדָמָה (adamah — 'ground'), and דָּם (dam — 'blood'). The war-horse is blood-colored — a Hebrew wordplay impossible in Greek where πυρρός ('fiery/flame-colored') has no connection to αἷμα ('blood') or ἄνθρωπος ('man'). A back-translator from πυρρός would use a fire-related word like אדמדם or אש-צבע, not the blood/earth root adom.

Hebrew says הַשָּׁלוֹם (ha-shalom — 'THE peace') with the definite article. Shalom in Hebrew encompasses wholeness, completeness, welfare, and covenant faithfulness — not merely the absence of war. Greek τὴν εἰρήνην ('the peace') is narrower. The Hebrew definite article suggests THE established shalom — the covenant order — is being removed.

Hebrew: הלך לחוץ (halakh la-chuts — 'went to the outside'). This decomposes the motion into verb + spatial adverb, a characteristically Hebrew construction. Greek ἐξῆλθεν is a single verb ('went out'). A back-translator would not decompose the Greek compound verb into this Hebrew spatial expression.
greek_deviations: Greek adds 'that they should slay one another' (ἵνα ἀλλήλους σφάξωσιν) — entirely absent from the Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'red' (adom — blood-colored). Greek: πυρρός ('fiery/flame-colored'). Different color associations.
translation_notes: חֶרֶב (cherev, H2719) — the standard Hebrew sword, the weapon of war throughout the OT (Gen 3:24, 27:40, Ex 5:21, Deut 32:25). Greek μάχαιρα can mean a knife or short sword.
textual_notes: Zechariah 1:8 and 6:2 — red horses appear in Zechariah's visions. In Zech 6:2, the red horses are paired with the first chariot. The Hebrew author draws from the same prophetic tradition.

verses.translation: And in the hour{H8160} that he opened{H6605} the third{H7992} seal{H2856}, the third{H7992} living-creature{H2416} said{H559}: Come{H935} and see{H7200}. And I saw{H7200} one{H259} black{H7838} horse{H5483}, and the one sitting{H3427} upon it had{H1961} in his hand{H3027} one{H259} set of scales{H3976}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁ (be-sha'ah she — 'in the hour that'). שָׁעָה in biblical Hebrew (H8159) means 'to gaze/look.' The meaning 'hour/time' is EXCLUSIVELY post-biblical/Mishnaic. This temporal expression is quintessentially Mishnaic — appearing constantly in Talmudic narrative. Greek ὅτε ('when') is simply a conjunction. A back-translator from Greek would use כאשר or בעת, not this Mishnaic time idiom. Like כיון ש in v.3, this proves living Hebrew composition.

Uses מֹאזְנַיִם (moznayim, H3976 — 'scales/balance'). This is a dual-form noun (the two pans of a balance), used in Leviticus 19:36 for just scales (מאזני צדק) and in Job 31:6 (ישקלני במאזני צדק — 'let him weigh me in just scales'). Greek ζυγόν (zygon) means 'yoke' and only secondarily 'balance beam.' A back-translator from Greek 'yoke' would not produce the specifically commercial/judicial Hebrew moznayim.
translation_notes: 'Scales' for moznayim — the dual form reflects the two-pan balance, an instrument of justice and commerce in the OT.
Gender mismatch persists: החיה (feminine) with השלישי (masculine ordinal). Consistent Mishnaic pattern throughout the chapter.
textual_notes: Black is the color of famine and mourning (Lam 4:8 — 'their appearance is blacker than soot'; Lam 5:10 — 'our skin was hot as an oven because of the burning heat of famine'). The scales indicate rationed food — famine conditions.

verses.translation: And I heard{H8085} one{H259} voice{H6963} in the midst{H8432} of the four{H702} living-creatures{H2416} saying{H559}: One{H259} measure{H4060} of wheat{H2406} for two{H8147} faces{H6440}, and three{H7969} measures{H4060} of barley{H8184} for two{H8147} faces{H6440}; and to the oil{H8081} and the wine{H3196} do not do{H6213} evil{H7451}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Hebrew uses פָּנִים (panim — 'faces', H6440) as the unit of price/currency. Greek uses δηναρίου ('a denarius' — a Roman coin). A back-translator from Greek would transliterate as דינר (dinar), NEVER produce פנים. The Hebrew author calls the coin denomination by its 'face' — because coins bear faces/images. This is a uniquely Semitic monetary idiom: the 'face' of the coin IS the coin. Compare how English preserves 'face value.' No translator going Greek→Hebrew would independently create this idiom.

Uses מִדָּה (middah, H4060 — 'measure') — a standard Hebrew volume/capacity measure. Greek χοῖνιξ (choinix) is a specific Greek dry measure (about a quart). A back-translator from Greek would transliterate the Greek unit, not substitute the generic Hebrew middah.

Uses אַל תַּעֲשֶׂה רַע (al ta'aseh ra — 'do not do evil') — the Hebrew moral vocabulary of רע (ra, H7451 — 'evil'). Greek μὴ ἀδικήσῃς ('do not act unjustly') uses the legal concept of ἀδικέω ('to wrong/injure'). A back-translator from Greek would write אל תעשה עוול ('do not do injustice'), not the general moral term ra ('evil'). The Hebrew frames the command in moral-cosmic terms; the Greek in legal terms.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'two faces' (panim — a monetary term). Greek: 'a denarius' (a specific Roman coin). Entirely different denomination system.
Hebrew: 'do not do evil' (moral framing). Greek: 'do not act unjustly' (legal framing).
translation_notes: 'Faces' for panim is preserved literally to show the Hebrew monetary idiom. The meaning is 'coins' — called by the face/image they bear.

חטים (chittim, H2406 — 'wheat') and שעורים (se'orim, H8184 — 'barley') are standard OT agricultural vocabulary. The price ratio (1 measure wheat = 3 measures barley) indicates severe famine prices — roughly 8-16 times normal.
textual_notes: Leviticus 26:26 — 'When I break your staff of bread, ten women shall bake your bread in one oven, and they shall deliver your bread by weight, and you shall eat and not be satisfied.' The famine-seal echoes Levitical covenant curses.
2 Kings 7:1 — Elisha's prophecy: 'a measure of fine flour for a shekel and two measures of barley for a shekel.' Similar commercial language for food pricing in famine/siege conditions.

verses.translation: And as soon as he opened{H6605} the fourth{H7243} seal{H2856}, I heard{H8085} the fourth{H7243} living-creature{H2416} saying{H559}: Come{H935} and see{H7200}.

one_way_hebrew: כיון ש (keivan she) again — the same Mishnaic conjunction as v.3, forming a consistent authorial pattern. A back-translator would not independently reproduce this idiom in multiple verses.
greek_deviations: Greek adds φωνήν ('a voice') — 'I heard a voice of the fourth living creature.' Hebrew simply: 'I heard the fourth living-creature saying.' Hebrew is more direct.

verses.translation: And I saw{H7200} one{H259} horse{H5483}, spotted{H1261} and strong{H553}, and the one who sits{H3427} upon it — his name{H8034} was Messenger{H4397} of Death{H4194}, and Gei-Hinnom went{H1980} after him{H310}. And to him was given{H5414} authority to kill{H4191} a fourth{H7243} part{H2506} upon the earth{H776}: by the sword{H2719} and by famine{H7458} and by pestilence{H4194} and by the hand{H3027} of the beasts{H2416} of the earth{H776}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses בָּרֹד (barod, H1261 — 'spotted/dappled') for the horse's color. Greek χλωρός (chloros — 'pale/greenish'). These are COMPLETELY different descriptions. Hebrew barod describes a mottled/speckled animal — the SAME word used in Genesis 31:10,12 for Jacob's spotted flocks and in Zechariah 6:3,6 for the dappled horses in the prophet's vision. A back-translator from Greek χλωρός would use ירקרק (yerakrak — 'greenish') or חִוֵּר (chiver — 'pale'). The use of barod ties this horse directly to Zechariah's four-horse vision.

Hebrew adds וְאַמֵּץ (ve-ametz — 'and strong', from אמץ H553). This word is entirely absent from Greek. It describes the horse's physical power/might — the word used when God tells Joshua 'be strong and courageous' (חזק ואמץ, Josh 1:6,7,9). No back-translator would add this.

CRITICAL: Uses מַלְאַךְ הַמָּוֶת (Malakh ha-Mavet — 'Messenger of Death', H4397 + H4194). This is the Angel of Death figure deeply embedded in Jewish tradition (2 Sam 24:16, Prov 16:14, Ps 78:49 traditions; extensively in Talmudic literature). Greek has simply Θάνατος ('Death'). A back-translator from Greek would write מָוֶת ('Death'), not the compound title 'Messenger of Death.' The Hebrew names a specific AGENT; the Greek names an abstract concept.

CRITICAL: Uses הַגֵּיהִנֹּם (ha-Geihinnom — 'Gei-Hinnom'). Greek has ᾍδης ('Hades'). Gei-Hinnom is the Valley of Hinnom — a REAL GEOGRAPHIC LOCATION south of Jerusalem (Josh 15:8, 18:16, 2 Kings 23:10, Jer 7:31-32, 19:2,6, 32:35) that became the site of child sacrifice to Molech and then the metaphor for divine judgment. Hades is the GREEK underworld. A back-translator from Greek ᾍδης would write שְׁאוֹל (Sheol — the Hebrew underworld equivalent), NEVER Gei-Hinnom. These are from completely different cultural-geographic frameworks.

Uses רְשׁוּת (reshut — 'authority/permission'). This is a quintessential MISHNAIC Hebrew term — the standard Talmudic word for legal authority/permission. It has no OT Hebrew equivalent (biblical Hebrew uses שלטון or ממשלה). Greek ἐξουσία ('authority') is standard. A back-translator would produce שלטון or ממשלה from ἐξουσία, not the Mishnaic reshut.

Uses the idiom עַל יַד (al yad — 'by the hand of', H5921 + H3027) for agency. This is a characteristically Hebrew expression for instrumentality. Greek ὑπό ('by/under') is a simple preposition. A back-translator would use ע״י or ב, not the fuller על יד.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'spotted and strong' (barod ve-ametz). Greek: 'pale/green' (chloros). Entirely different description. Greek lacks 'strong.'
Hebrew: 'Messenger of Death' (compound title). Greek: 'Death' (simple name).
Hebrew: 'Gei-Hinnom' (geographic). Greek: 'Hades' (mythological). Different conceptual worlds.

Hebrew: 'authority' (reshut — Mishnaic). Greek: 'authority' (exousia) + 'over a fourth of the earth' (ἐπὶ τὸ τέταρτον τῆς γῆς). Greek frames authority as 'over' territory; Hebrew frames it as authority 'to kill a fourth portion upon the earth.'
translation_notes: 'Pestilence' for mavet in the list (sword, famine, pestilence, beasts). In OT prophetic usage, mavet ('death') in a list of plagues means 'pestilence/plague' — see Jeremiah 15:2: 'those destined for pestilence (mavet), to pestilence; those destined for the sword, to the sword; those destined for famine, to famine' and Ezekiel 14:21.
'Spotted' for barod — following the Zechariah horse vision tradition rather than the Greek 'pale' interpretation.
textual_notes: Ezekiel 14:21 — 'my four deadly acts of judgment: sword, famine, wild beasts, and pestilence.' The Hebrew Revelation's four-fold judgment (sword, famine, pestilence, beasts) matches Ezekiel's four judgments EXACTLY in the same categories, though in different order. This is standard OT prophetic language that the Hebrew author naturally employs.

Zechariah 6:1-8 — four chariots with different-colored horses. The Hebrew Revelation's four horses echo Zechariah's four horse teams, with the 'spotted' (barod) horse directly matching Zechariah's ברדים (beruddim — 'dappled/spotted') horses.

verses.translation: And as soon as he opened{H6605} the fifth{H2549}, I saw{H7200} beneath{H8478} the sanctuary{H1964} the breaths{H5397} that were slain{H2026} for the sanctification{H6944} of YHWH{H3068}, and for the sake of the testimony{H5715} that they had{H1961}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses הֵיכָל (heikhal, H1964 — 'sanctuary/palace'). This is the specific word for the inner Temple — the nave of Solomon's Temple (1 Kings 6:3,5,17,33; 7:50), the heavenly temple (Ps 11:4, 18:6, Hab 2:20, Mic 1:2). Greek has θυσιαστηρίου (thysiasteriou — 'altar'). These are ENTIRELY DIFFERENT sacred spaces. The souls are beneath the SANCTUARY (the holy place where God dwells) in the Hebrew, but beneath the ALTAR (where sacrifices are offered) in the Greek. A back-translator from Greek would write מזבח (mizbeach — 'altar'), NEVER היכל. The Hebrew implies the souls dwell in God's heavenly palace; the Greek implies they are sacrificial offerings.

CRITICAL: Uses עַל קְדוּשַּׁת יַהְוֶה (al kedushat YHWH — 'for the sanctification of YHWH'). This is the concept of קִדּוּשׁ הַשֵּׁם (kiddush ha-Shem — 'sanctification of the Name') — THE specifically Jewish concept of martyrdom, dying to sanctify God's name. This concept pervades Rabbinic literature and became the standard term for Jewish martyrdom. Greek has διὰ τὸν λόγον τοῦ θεοῦ ('for the word of God'). A back-translator from Greek would write על דבר אלהים ('for the word of God'), NEVER produce the technical kiddush ha-Shem concept. This is one of the chapter's strongest one-way markers.

Uses נְשָׁמוֹת (neshamot — 'breaths/souls', H5397), from the root נשם ('to breathe'). This is THE word from Genesis 2:7 — נִשְׁמַת חַיִּים (nishmat chayyim — 'breath of life') that God breathed into Adam. Greek uses ψυχάς (psychas — 'souls'). A back-translator from Greek ψυχή would use נפשות (nefashot — from nephesh, the standard Hebrew equivalent of psyche). The use of neshamah rather than nephesh implies the divine-breath component of the soul — these are bearers of God's own breath.

Uses בִּשְׁבִיל (bishvil — 'for the sake of') — a quintessential MISHNAIC Hebrew preposition meaning 'because of/for the sake of.' It appears nowhere in the OT. Greek διά ('because of/for') is standard. A back-translator from Greek would use למען, בגלל, or בעבור — biblical Hebrew causal prepositions. The Mishnaic bishvil further confirms living Hebrew composition.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'beneath the sanctuary' (היכל — heavenly palace). Greek: 'beneath the altar' (θυσιαστηρίου). Different sacred architecture.
Hebrew: 'for the sanctification of YHWH' (kiddush ha-Shem martyrdom concept). Greek: 'for the word of God' (logos tou theou). Different reason for dying.
Hebrew: neshamot ('divine breaths/souls'). Greek: psychas ('souls'). Different anthropological term.
translation_notes: 'Breaths' for neshamot to preserve the Genesis 2:7 connection — these are bearers of God's own nishmat chayyim.
'Sanctification' for kedushat to capture the kiddush ha-Shem concept. These are martyrs who died to sanctify God's name.
עֵדוּת (edut, H5715 — 'testimony') — the same word for the Tablets of Testimony (לוחות העדות, Ex 31:18, 32:15, 34:29) and the Ark of the Testimony. The martyrs bore witness like the Torah tablets.
textual_notes: The location 'beneath the sanctuary' connects to the ancient Jewish concept that the souls of the righteous are stored 'under the throne of glory' (תחת כסא הכבוד — Shabbat 152b). The Hebrew naturally places martyred souls beneath God's heavenly dwelling.

verses.translation: And they were crying out{H6817} with a great{H1419} voice{H6963} and saying{H559}: Master{H113}, the Holy{H6918} and the Faithful{H539}, until when{H4970} will you judge{H8199} and not avenge{H5358} our blood{H1818} from those who dwell upon the earth{H776}?

one_way_hebrew: Uses צוֹעֲקִים (tso'akim — 'crying out', from צעק H6817). This is THE word for Israel's cry of distress from Egypt: וַיִּצְעֲקוּ ('and they cried out', Ex 2:23, 14:10). It recurs throughout Judges when Israel cries out under oppression (Judg 3:9, 3:15, 4:3, 6:6, 10:10). The martyrs' cry uses the Exodus vocabulary of oppression. Greek ἔκραξαν (from κράζω) is generic 'they shouted.' A back-translator would use זעק (za'aq) or קרא (qara), not specifically the Exodus-laden צעק.

Uses נֶאֱמָן (ne'eman — 'faithful/trustworthy', from אמן H539). Greek has ἀληθινός (alethinos — 'true/genuine'). A back-translator from Greek ἀληθινός would use אֲמִתִּי (amitti — 'true') or אֶמֶת (emet — 'truth'). The Hebrew ne'eman means 'faithful/reliable' — a DIFFERENT theological attribute from 'true.' God is called ne'eman in Deuteronomy 7:9 (הָאֵל הַנֶּאֱמָן — 'the faithful God'). The Hebrew invokes covenant faithfulness; the Greek invokes ontological truthfulness.

Hebrew: עד מתי תשפוט ואינה תנקם — 'until when will you judge and NOT avenge.' This implies God IS judging but has NOT YET avenged. Greek: Ἕως πότε... οὐ κρίνεις καὶ ἐκδικεῖς — 'until when do you NOT judge AND avenge.' Greek implies God is doing NEITHER. These are different theological claims about divine activity.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'faithful' (ne'eman — covenant loyalty). Greek: 'true' (alethinos — genuineness). Different divine attribute.
Hebrew implies God is judging but not yet avenging. Greek implies God is doing neither.
Hebrew: 'those who dwell' (דרים — Mishnaic present participle of דור). Greek: κατοικούντων ('inhabitants'). The Hebrew דרים (darim) is a Mishnaic form; biblical Hebrew would use ישבים (yoshvim).
translation_notes: 'Master' for adon (H113) — not YHWH but the title of sovereign authority. Psalm 12:4 and Psalm 114:7 use this form.

Blood vengeance (נקם דם) is a foundational OT concept: Genesis 4:10 — Abel's blood 'cries out from the ground'; Deuteronomy 32:43 — 'he avenges the blood of his servants'; Psalm 79:10 — 'let the avenging of the blood of your servants be known among the nations.'
textual_notes: The cry עד מתי ('until when/how long') echoes Psalm 13:1-2 — 'How long, O YHWH? Will you forget me forever?' and Psalm 79:5 — 'How long, O YHWH? Will you be angry forever?' and Habakkuk 1:2 — 'O YHWH, how long shall I cry and you will not hear?' The martyrs cry with the Psalms' vocabulary.

verses.translation: And to each{H3605} one{H259} of them was given{H5414} white{H3836} garments{H4403}, and it was said{H559} to them that they should be still{H8252} yet{H5750} a small{H4592} time.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מַלְבּוּשֵׁי (malbushei — 'garments of', from לבש H3847, noun form H4403). This word emphasizes the act of being clothed — it is the garment-as-worn, used for royal garments (1 Kings 10:5, 2 Chr 9:4, Ezek 16:13). Greek στολαί ('robes') is a specific type of robe. A back-translator from Greek would use בגדים (begadim — 'garments') or כתנות (ketonot — 'tunics'), not the specifically royal/dignified malbushim.

Uses תִּשְׁקְטוּ (tishketu — 'be still/at rest', from שקט H8252). This is the word for the land being at rest after war: 'the land had rest (שקט) forty years' (Judg 3:11, 3:30, 5:31, 8:28). It implies CESSATION OF STRIFE — the martyrs should rest from their cry for vengeance as one rests from battle. Greek ἀναπαύσωνται ('rest/take repose') is generic rest. A back-translator from Greek would use ינוחו (yanuchu — 'rest', from נוח), not the war-ceasefire verb shaqat.

Uses זְמָן (zeman — 'a time'). This is a distinctly post-biblical/Mishnaic word for 'time/appointed time.' Biblical Hebrew uses עת (et) or מועד (mo'ed). Greek χρόνον ('time') is standard. A back-translator from Greek would use עת or זמן (less likely the latter, but the consistent use of Mishnaic vocabulary throughout confirms Hebrew composition).
greek_deviations: MAJOR: Greek adds an entire clause absent from Hebrew: ἕως πληρωθῶσιν καὶ οἱ σύνδουλοι αὐτῶν καὶ οἱ ἀδελφοὶ αὐτῶν, οἱ μέλλοντες ἀποκτέννεσθαι ὡς καὶ αὐτοί ('until their fellow servants and brothers who were about to be killed as they were should be complete'). This entire clause about future martyrs is absent from the Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'be still' (שקט — cease from agitation). Greek: 'rest' (ἀναπαύω — take repose). Different type of quietness.
translation_notes: 'Be still' for shaqat captures the military-rest nuance — these are warriors told to stand down, not sleepers told to nap.
'Garments' for malbushim — the dignified/royal garment, clothing the martyrs in honor.

verses.translation: And I saw{H7200} that he opened{H6605} the sixth{H8345}, and there was a trembling{H7461} of the earth{H776}, and the sun{H8121} was{H1961} black{H7838}, and the moon{H3394} was{H1961} red{H122} as blood{H1818}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses רַעֲדוֹת הָאָרֶץ (ra'adot ha-aretz — 'trembling of the earth', from רעד H7460). The noun רַעֲדָה (re'adah, H7461) describes personal trembling from fear/awe: 'serve YHWH with fear and rejoice with trembling (רעדה)' (Ps 2:11); 'trembling (רעדה) seized the godless' (Isa 33:14). The Hebrew personifies the earth as TREMBLING IN FEAR. Greek σεισμὸς μέγας ('a great earthquake') is a technical geological term. A back-translator from Greek would use רעש גדול (ra'ash gadol — 'great earthquake'), using the standard Hebrew earthquake word רעש, not the fear-trembling word רעדה.

Hebrew: אדם כדם (adom ka-dam — 'red as blood'). The wordplay between אדם (adom — 'red') and דם (dam — 'blood') involves the same consonantal root א-ד-ם. The moon becomes 'blood-red' with the Hebrew pun embedded. Greek simply says ὡς αἷμα ('as blood') without the color word. The Hebrew is richer.
Hebrew lacks 'great' (μέγας) before the earthquake. Greek says 'a GREAT earthquake.' The Hebrew simply records 'a trembling of the earth' without magnifying it.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'trembling of the earth' (personified fear). Greek: 'a great earthquake' (geological event + adjective 'great').
Greek adds ὡς σάκκος τρίχινος ('like a hairy sackcloth') after 'the sun was black.' This simile is absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'red as blood' (with adom/dam wordplay). Greek: simply 'as blood' (no color word).
translation_notes: 'Trembling' for ra'adot preserves the personification — the earth itself trembles, like a person trembling before God.
textual_notes: Joel 2:31 (Hebrew 3:4) — הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ יֵהָפֵךְ לְחֹשֶׁךְ וְהַיָּרֵחַ לְדָם ('The sun shall be turned to darkness and the moon to blood'). The Hebrew Revelation echoes Joel's cosmic signs. Joel says 'darkness' (חשך); the Hebrew Revelation says 'black' (שחור) — a related but different word. The moon-blood connection is preserved directly.
Isaiah 13:10 — 'The sun will be dark (חשך) at its rising, and the moon will not shed its light.' Cosmic darkening as a sign of YHWH's day of judgment.

verses.translation: And all{H3605} their host{H6635} shall wither{H5034} as a leaf{H5929} withers{H5034} from a vine{H1612}, and as a withered-fig{H5034} from a fig-tree{H8384}.

one_way_hebrew: VERBATIM ISAIAH QUOTE: This verse is taken almost word-for-word from Isaiah 34:4b — וְכָל צְבָאָם יִבּוֹל כִּנְבֹל עָלֶה מִגֶּפֶן וּכְנֹבֶלֶת מִתְּאֵנָה ('and all their host shall wither as a leaf withers from a vine, and as a withered-fig from a fig-tree'). The match is EXACT. Greek has 'the stars of heaven fell to the earth, as a fig tree casts its unripe figs when shaken by a great wind' (οἱ ἀστέρες τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ἔπεσον εἰς τὴν γῆν, ὡς συκῆ βάλλει τοὺς ὀλύνθους αὐτῆς ὑπὸ ἀνέμου μεγάλου σειομένη). A back-translator from Greek would write כוכבי השמים נפלו ארצה כתאנה משלכת פגיה ברוח גדולה — bearing NO resemblance to Isaiah 34:4. The Hebrew PRESERVES the Isaiah source text; the Greek PARAPHRASES it.

Uses צְבָאָם (tseva'am — 'their host', H6635). Hebrew צבא is the cosmic-military term for the heavenly host — stars conceived as an army (Gen 2:1, Deut 4:19, Isa 34:4, 40:26). Greek has ἀστέρες τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ('stars of heaven'). The Hebrew author uses the OT cosmic-military term; the Greek translator made it explicit with 'stars of heaven.'

The verb יִבּוֹל (yibol — 'shall wither/fade', H5034) and כנבל (kinvol — 'as withers') and כנבלת (ke-novelet — 'as a withered-thing') all derive from the root נבל (navel — 'to wither/fade/fall'). This triple use of the same root creates alliterative emphasis impossible in the Greek, which uses three different verbs (ἔπεσον 'fell', βάλλει 'casts', σειομένη 'shaken').
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'all their host shall wither' (Isaiah 34:4 verbatim). Greek: 'the stars of heaven fell to the earth.' Different verb, different subject.

Hebrew: 'as a leaf withers from a vine, and as a withered-fig from a fig-tree' (Isaiah 34:4). Greek: 'as a fig-tree casts its unripe figs when shaken by a great wind.' Different imagery — Hebrew emphasizes withering; Greek emphasizes violent shaking.
Greek adds 'stars fell to the earth' and 'shaken by a great wind' — both absent from Hebrew.
translation_notes: 'Host' for tsava — preserving the military/cosmic nuance. The heavenly bodies are God's army.
'Withered-fig' for novelet — a feminine participial form meaning 'a withered/fallen thing,' specifically an overripe fig that drops from the tree.
textual_notes: Isaiah 34:4 (full verse): וְנָמַקּוּ כָּל צְבָא הַשָּׁמַיִם וְנָגֹלּוּ כַסֵּפֶר הַשָּׁמָיִם וְכָל צְבָאָם יִבּוֹל כִּנְבֹל עָלֶה מִגֶּפֶן וּכְנֹבֶלֶת מִתְּאֵנָה — 'And all the host of heaven shall waste away, and the heavens shall be rolled up like a scroll, and all their host shall wither as a leaf withers from a vine and as a withered-fig from a fig-tree.' The Hebrew Revelation quotes the second half verbatim. This is one of the strongest one-way markers in the chapter.

verses.translation: And all{H3605} the mountains{H2022} and hills{H1389} were shaken from their place{H4725}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses הָרִים וּגְבָעוֹת (harim u-geva'ot — 'mountains and hills'). This is standard OT prophetic pairing: Isaiah 2:14 ('upon all the high mountains and upon all the lifted hills'), Isaiah 40:4 ('every mountain and hill shall be made low'), Isaiah 54:10 ('though the mountains depart and the hills be shaken'), Micah 6:1 ('arise, contend before the mountains, and let the hills hear your voice'). Greek has ὄρος καὶ νῆσος ('mountain and island'). A back-translator from Greek would write הר ואי ('mountain and island'), NEVER substitute 'hills' (גבעות) for 'islands' (νῆσος). The Hebrew preserves the OT prophetic pairing; the Greek transforms hills into islands.

The verb נִדַּעֲזוּ (nid'azu — 'were shaken') appears to be a rare or dialectal Hebrew form. It may derive from a root related to זעזע (za'aza — 'to shake violently') with an infixed ד, or from an otherwise unattested root דעז. Its rarity suggests genuine Hebrew composition rather than back-translation, where a translator would use the common biblical word נמוטו (namotu — 'were shaken') or הוזזו (huzazu — 'were moved').
greek_deviations: MAJOR: Hebrew lacks the entire clause: ὁ οὐρανὸς ἀπεχωρίσθη ὡς βιβλίον ἑλισσόμενον ('the heaven departed as a scroll rolled up'). This is present in Greek but absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'mountains and hills' (הרים וגבעות). Greek: 'mountain and island' (ὄρος καὶ νῆσος). Different second element.
translation_notes: נדעזו is a hapax or extremely rare form. 'Were shaken' captures the evident meaning from context. The form may reflect dialectal or colloquial Hebrew.
textual_notes: Isaiah 54:10 — כִּי הֶהָרִים יָמוּשׁוּ וְהַגְּבָעוֹת תְּמוּטֶינָה ('though the mountains depart and the hills be shaken'). The Hebrew Revelation uses the same mountain-hill pair in the same context of cosmic upheaval.

Note that Isaiah 34:4a (the first half of the verse partially quoted in v.13) says 'the heavens shall be rolled up like a scroll' (ונגלו כספר השמים). The Hebrew Revelation omits this; the Greek preserves it. This suggests the Hebrew author selectively quoted Isaiah 34.

verses.translation: And kings{H4428} of the earth{H776} and rulers{H7336} and the wealthy{H6223} and the officers{H7860} and the servants{H5650} and the free ones{H2670} were hiding{H5641} in caves{H4631} of rocks{H6697} and in tunnels{H4247} of dust{H6083}.

one_way_hebrew: VERBATIM ISAIAH QUOTE: בִּמְעָרוֹת צֻרִים וּבִמְחִלּוֹת עָפָר ('in caves of rocks and in tunnels of dust') is taken directly from Isaiah 2:19 — וּבָאוּ בִּמְעָרוֹת צֻרִים וּבִמְחִלּוֹת עָפָר מִפְּנֵי פַּחַד יְהוָה וּמֵהֲדַר גְּאוֹנוֹ ('and they shall go into caves of rocks and tunnels of dust from before the terror of YHWH and the splendor of his majesty'). The Hebrew preserves Isaiah's EXACT phrasing. Greek has εἰς τὰ σπήλαια καὶ εἰς τὰς πέτρας τῶν ὀρέων ('into the caves and into the rocks of the mountains'). A back-translator from Greek would write במערות ובסלעי ההרים ('in caves and in the rocks of the mountains'), NOT the Isaiah-specific 'tunnels of dust' (מחילות עפר).

Uses רוֹזְנִים (rozenim — 'rulers/dignitaries', H7336). This is an archaic/poetic Hebrew word appearing in Judges 5:3, Psalm 2:2, Proverbs 8:15, 31:4, Isaiah 40:23, Habakkuk 1:10. The pairing מלכי ארץ ורוזנים ('kings of the earth and rulers') directly echoes Psalm 2:2 — יִתְיַצְּבוּ מַלְכֵי אֶרֶץ וְרוֹזְנִים ('the kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers'). Greek μεγιστᾶνες ('great men/magnates') is generic. A back-translator from Greek would use גדולים or שרים, not the archaic Psalm 2 term rozenim.

Uses שׁוֹטְרִים (shotrim — 'officers', H7860). This is a specifically Israelite administrative term for foremen/officials (Ex 5:6,10,14; Deut 1:15, 16:18, 20:5,8,9; Josh 1:10). These are the officers who organized Israel's tribal administration. Greek χιλίαρχοι ('commanders of a thousand') is a Greco-Roman military rank. A back-translator from Greek would write שרי אלפים ('captains of thousands') to mirror the Greek term, not the Torah-specific shotrim.
greek_deviations: Hebrew list: kings, rulers, wealthy, officers, servants, free (6 categories). Greek list: kings, great men, commanders, rich, strong, every slave, every free (7 categories). Greek adds 'strong' (ἰσχυροί) absent from Hebrew.
Hebrew: 'caves of rocks and tunnels of dust' (Isaiah 2:19 verbatim). Greek: 'caves and rocks of the mountains.' Different hiding places.
Hebrew: 'rulers' (rozenim — archaic/Psalm 2). Greek: 'great men' (megistanes). Different social category.
translation_notes: 'Rulers' for rozenim — preserving the Psalm 2 connection and the archaic Hebrew dignity of the term.
'Officers' for shotrim — the Israelite tribal administrative officials, not Roman military commanders.
'Tunnels of dust' for mechilot afar — underground passages in the dry earth, distinct from rocky caves.
textual_notes: Isaiah 2:19-21 is the direct source: 'And they shall go into caves of rocks and tunnels of dust, from before the terror of YHWH and from the splendor of his majesty, when he rises to terrify the earth.' The Hebrew Revelation quotes this passage and then extends it in verses 16-17.

Psalm 2:2 — 'The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers (rozenim) take counsel together against YHWH and against his anointed.' The Psalm 2 language of kings and rulers rebelling against God's authority frames the entire passage.

verses.translation: And saying{H559} to the mountains{H2022} and to the rocks{H5553}: Fall{H5307} upon us and hide{H5641} us from the face{H6440} of the appearance{H4758} of the one sitting{H3427} upon the throne{H3678}, and from the burning-wrath{H2740} of the lamb{H7716}.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew adds הַמַּרְאֶה (ha-mar'eh — 'the appearance/vision', H4758) — entirely absent from Greek. In Ezekiel, God's presence is repeatedly described as a מַרְאֶה (mar'eh — 'appearance/vision'): Ezekiel 1:26-28 ('the appearance of the likeness of the glory of YHWH'), Ezekiel 8:2 ('the appearance of fire'), Ezekiel 10:1. This is an Ezekiel-specific term for theophany. A back-translator from Greek, which has simply ἀπὸ προσώπου τοῦ καθημένου ('from the face of the one sitting'), would not add this Ezekiel technical term.

Uses חֲרוֹן (charon, H2740 — 'burning-wrath'), specifically the fierce/burning anger of God. This word appears 40+ times in the OT (Ex 32:12, Num 25:4, Deut 13:17, Josh 7:26, 2 Kings 23:26, Jer 4:8). Greek ὀργῆς (orges — 'anger/wrath') is generic. A back-translator from Greek would use אף (af), חמה (chemah), or עברה (evrah), not the specific charon which typically pairs with af as חרון אף ('burning of anger') in the OT. The use of charon alone is theologically loaded — it is the BURNING quality of divine wrath.

The phrase מפני ('from the face of') used twice — מפני המראה של זה היושב... ומפני חרון — echoes Isaiah 2:19,21 where the same preposition frames divine terror: מפני פחד יהוה ('from the face of the terror of YHWH'). The Hebrew Revelation continues the Isaiah 2 quotation begun in v.15.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'from the face of the APPEARANCE of the one sitting' (adds mar'eh — theophany term). Greek: 'from the face of the one sitting' (no 'appearance').
Hebrew: 'burning-wrath' (charon — specific burning anger). Greek: 'wrath' (orge — generic anger).
translation_notes: 'Burning-wrath' for charon — this is not merely anger but the burning/fierce quality of divine anger, a technical prophetic term.
'Appearance' for mar'eh — the theophanic vision, how God manifests visibly. These people flee not from God directly but from the visible manifestation of his presence.
textual_notes: Hosea 10:8 — וְאָמְרוּ לֶהָרִים כַּסּוּנוּ וְלַגְּבָעוֹת נִפְלוּ עָלֵינוּ ('and they shall say to the mountains: Cover us, and to the hills: Fall on us'). The Hebrew Revelation echoes Hosea but uses סלעים ('rocks') where Hosea has גבעות ('hills'). Yeshua quotes this Hosea passage in Luke 23:30.

The combined quotation of Isaiah 2:19 (v.15) + Hosea 10:8 (v.16) shows the Hebrew author weaving OT prophetic texts together — a technique characteristic of Hebrew literary composition, not translation.

verses.translation: For the day{H3117} of the burning{H2740} of his nostril{H639} has come{H935}, and who{H4310} is able{H3201} to stand{H5975} before him{H6440}?

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses חֲרוֹן אַפּוֹ (charon apo — 'the burning of his nostril', H2740 + H639). This is THE standard OT expression for God's fierce anger — an anthropomorphism of God's nostrils flaring with burning wrath. It appears in: Exodus 32:12 ('turn from the burning of your anger'), Numbers 25:4, Deuteronomy 13:17, Joshua 7:26, 2 Kings 23:26, Isaiah 13:9,13, Jeremiah 4:8, 12:13, 25:37, 30:24, 51:45, Lamentations 1:12, 2:1,3, Nahum 1:6, Zephaniah 2:2-3, 3:8, and many more. Greek has ἡ ἡμέρα ἡ μεγάλη τῆς ὀργῆς αὐτοῦ ('the great day of HIS WRATH'). A back-translator from Greek would write יום חרון אפו or more likely יום הגדול של זעמו — but the Hebrew construction 'the day of the burning of his nostril' is the deeply embedded OT prophetic formula that a translator would not independently reconstruct from the Greek. The anthropomorphism (God's nostrils) is uniquely Hebrew.

Hebrew lacks 'great' (μεγάλη). Greek says 'the GREAT day of his wrath.' Hebrew simply says 'the day of his burning-nostril.' The Hebrew is more intimate and visceral; the Greek adds an adjective of magnitude.

Uses מִי יוּכַל לַעֲמוֹד לְפָנָיו ('who is able to stand before him') — the OT idiom עמד לפני (amad lifnei — 'to stand before') denoting being in someone's presence/service (Gen 41:46, 1 Sam 16:22, 1 Kings 1:2, Jer 15:19). This echoes Nahum 1:6: מִי יַעֲמוֹד לִפְנֵי זַעְמוֹ ('who can stand before his fury?') and Malachi 3:2: וּמִי הָעֹמֵד בְּהֵרָאוֹתוֹ ('who can stand when he appears?'). The Hebrew weaves Nahum and Malachi together naturally. Greek σταθῆναι is simply 'to stand' without the interpersonal 'before his face' nuance.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'the day of the burning of his nostril' (anthropomorphic — God's nostrils flare). Greek: 'the great day of his wrath' (abstract — magnitude of anger + 'great').
Hebrew: no adjective modifying 'day.' Greek: adds 'great' (μεγάλη).

Greek: τῆς ὀργῆς αὐτοῦ ('of his wrath'). But whose wrath? Greek is ambiguous — it could refer to the one on the throne or the lamb. Hebrew: אפו ('his nostril') with singular suffix, naturally referring to the one on the throne.
translation_notes: 'Burning of his nostril' preserves the Hebrew anthropomorphism. אף (af, H639) literally means 'nose/nostril' and by extension 'anger' (because nostrils flare in anger). חרון אף is literally 'the burning of the nose' — God's nostrils are hot with fury.
'To stand before him' — the language of royal audience. Who can maintain their standing (position/status/courage) in the presence of such wrath?
textual_notes: Nahum 1:6 — לִפְנֵי זַעְמוֹ מִי יַעֲמוֹד וּמִי יָקוּם בַּחֲרוֹן אַפּוֹ ('Before his rage who can stand, and who can rise up against the burning of his anger?'). The Hebrew Revelation combines Nahum's חרון אפו with his מי יעמוד in a single sentence.

Malachi 3:2 — וּמִי מְכַלְכֵּל אֶת יוֹם בּוֹאוֹ וּמִי הָעֹמֵד בְּהֵרָאוֹתוֹ ('And who can endure the day of his coming? And who can stand when he appears?'). The 'day + coming + who can stand' structure is preserved in the Hebrew Revelation.
Zephaniah 2:2-3 — בְּטֶרֶם לֹא בָּא עֲלֵיכֶם חֲרוֹן אַף יְהוָה ('before the burning of YHWH's anger comes upon you'). The same charon af + bo (come) construction.

chapter_notes.summary:
Revelation 6 in Hebrew is saturated with OT prophetic quotations and Mishnaic Hebrew features that could not arise from back-translation of the Greek text. The chapter contains at least 20 clear one-way translation markers.

The strongest one-way markers are: (1) VERBATIM QUOTE of Isaiah 34:4 in v.13, where the Hebrew matches the OT word-for-word while the Greek paraphrases freely; (2) VERBATIM QUOTE of Isaiah 2:19 in v.15, using the distinctly Isaiah 'tunnels of dust' (מחילות עפר) where Greek has generic 'rocks of the mountains'; (3) מלאך המות (Malakh ha-Mavet — 'Messenger of Death') vs. Greek 'Death' — the Hebrew names the Jewish angelic figure; (4) גיהנם (Gei-Hinnom) vs. Greek Hades — a geographic Hebrew location vs. the Greek mythological underworld; (5) היכל (heikhal — 'sanctuary') vs. Greek 'altar' — entirely different sacred architecture; (6) קדושת יהוה (kedushat YHWH — 'sanctification of YHWH') — the technical kiddush ha-Shem martyrdom concept vs. Greek 'word of God'; (7) פנים (panim — 'faces') for currency vs. Greek 'denarius'; (8) ברד (barod — 'spotted') vs. Greek chloros ('pale'), connecting to Zechariah's horse visions; (9) חרון אפו ('burning of his nostril') — the OT anthropomorphic wrath formula vs. Greek 'the great day of his wrath'; (10) רוזנים (rozenim — 'rulers') from Psalm 2:2.

Mishnaic Hebrew features pervade the text: כיון ש (keivan she — 'as soon as', vv.3,7), בשעה ש (be-sha'ah she — 'in the hour that', v.5), בשביל (bishvil — 'for the sake of', v.9), רשות (reshut — 'authority', v.8), זמן (zeman — 'time', v.11), דרים (darim — 'dwelling', v.10), and consistent masculine-for-feminine gender relaxation in participles. These are living Hebrew speech patterns that no Greek back-translator would produce.

The four horsemen sequence draws systematically from Zechariah 1:8 and 6:1-8 (colored horses), Ezekiel 14:21 (sword, famine, pestilence, beasts — the four judgments), and the Isaiah 2/34 Day of YHWH tradition. The fifth seal introduces specifically Jewish martyrdom theology (kiddush ha-Shem). The sixth seal weaves Joel 2:31, Isaiah 34:4, Isaiah 2:19, Hosea 10:8, Nahum 1:6, and Malachi 3:2 into a unified vision of cosmic judgment — all using the OT Hebrew source texts directly.
